newsitem.title: USA: CME seen opening GFX arbitrage arm in late January.
newsitem.headline: CME seen opening GFX arbitrage arm in late January.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) plans to open its GLOBEX Foreign Exchange Facility (GFX) on January 23 and will probably announce this start date within days, exchange sources said.
"Absolutely, that's (January 23) the date," said one exchange source close to the unit, which will officially begin operations that day at 1430 CST/2030 GMT.
The GFX board will meet this afternoon and decide how to handle opening-day details, including the media coverage, the source added.
"I think we are going to be ready to announce a launch date, maybe even this week," a CME spokeswoman said in response to an inquiry. "I think it (the date) is going to be late January."
Michael Dengis, GFX managing director, declined comment.
Sources said the futures-cash currency arbitrage unit has been quietly trading limited amounts of cash and futures in marks and yen for several weeks on a pilot basis.
GLOBEX is an electronic trading system owned by the CME, Reuters Holdings Plc, and the Marche a Terme International de France. The CME alone owns GFX.

The sources said GFX would start without benefit of the most advanced state-of-the-art order matching or foreign exchange dealing systems, the lack of which they said would slow GFX's ability to conduct the most effective arbitrage.
"What they do have is a lot more counterparties than the average EFP (exchange-for-physicals) house would have," one source said.
The CME conceived GFX to pump up liquidity in GLOBEX after-hours electronic currency trading in hopes that volume also would flow to currency futures pits on the trading floor.

Volume last year in CME currency futures and futures-options slipped 2.5 percent from 1995, continuing erosion that has eaten into turnover in that complex over the last several years as the cash and EFP markets have grown.

Under GFX, which the CME bankrolled with an estimated $7 million of exchange money, two shifts of CME traders make two-way markets in the futures markets and quickly hedge them in the cash market, a theoretically low-risk arbitrage.

The CME hopes to make GLOBEX liquid enough and its bid/ask spreads tight enough to recapture business lost to the EFP market, exchange officials have said. ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750/E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com))
